summary: A Network Host Status report covering June 19 to June 30, 1972. No testing was done on June 20 because of an attempt to install the new IMP system. It was replaced by RFC 367.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

subtitle: Checking which network hosts were working in late June 1972

tldr.problem: Users needed current status of ARPANET host availability.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested network hosts from June 19 to June 30, 1972. No testing was done on June 20 due to an IMP system installation attempt.
tldr.outcome: The report captures a snapshot of the ARPANET near the end of June 1972, showing mature operational patterns across the network.

today: RFC 367 replaced this status report in July 1972. These early host status reports provided the first systematic view of distributed network operations in computing history.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 366 reports on host status from June 19 to June 30, 1972. By this time, the ARPANET had matured significantly since its founding five years earlier. No testing was done on June 20 due to an attempt to install the new IMP system. This report represents the final piece of the early host status survey series, documenting the network's state at the end of June 1972.
sections.plainLanguage: This report shows how the ARPANET was doing near the end of June 1972. The network was now well established, with regular operations across many sites.

sections.title: Network Structure
sections.content:
By June 30, 1972, the user-only hosts excluded from testing included Terminal IMPs at AMES, MITRE, RADC, NBS, ETAC, USC, GWC, NOAA, SAAC, ARPA, and BBN, plus the Network Control Center (Address 5). The operational servers included UCLA, SRI (two sites), UCSB, UTAH, MIT (four sites), RAND, SDC, Harvard, Lincoln (two sites), Stanford, Case (which had become a server in late June), Carnegie, and AMES.

This represented a comprehensive distributed computing network, with multiple sites offering different services and capabilities to ARPANET users nationwide.
sections.plainLanguage: The network now had many different computers in different cities all working together. Some were just connection points (Terminal IMPs), while others offered services that other people could use.

sections.title: Network Status and Performance
sections.content:
The testing shows predominantly Open status for most operational servers. UCLA, UCSB, MIT-Multics, MIT-DM, MIT-AI, MIT-ML, RAND, Harvard, Stanford, Carnegie, and AMES-ILLIAC frequently achieved Open status, indicating reliable connectivity. Some hosts like SRI-AI remained persistently dead or problematic.

The network showed the stability expected of an operational system after five years of development. Temporary failures occurred, but the core infrastructure was sound. The ARPANET had transitioned from an experimental network to an operational resource serving the research community.
sections.plainLanguage: Most computers were working pretty well by the end of June. A few still had problems, but overall the network was reliable and useful for research.
